entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Guan Xing (courtesy name Anguo) was a prominent military officer and official of the state of Shu Han during China's tumultuous Three Kingdoms period (220–280 CE), dying in 234 CE. As the second son of the revered general Guan Yu and brother to Guan Ping, Guan Xing inherited a legacy deeply entwined with the foundation and martial prowess of Shu Han. His career, though relatively short, saw him participate in key campaigns to solidify Shu's position against the rival states of Wei and Wu, particularly under the regency of Zhuge Liang. He represents the second generation of leadership tasked with maintaining the vision of Liu Bei's empire amidst constant warfare and political intrigue, embodying the Confucian ideals of loyalty and filial piety within a military context.

Historical records, primarily Chen Shou's 3rd-century "Records of the Three Kingdoms" (Sanguozhi), indicate that Guan Xing held the position of Palace Assistant Imperial Clerk and later Administrator of Hanchang Commandery, demonstrating his administrative capabilities alongside his military duties. He was renowned for his intelligence and diligence, qualities that earned him the high regard of the chancellor Zhuge Liang. While specific battlefield exploits are less detailed than those of his father, his presence in the Shu Han court and military command structure was crucial for maintaining morale and continuity, especially after the devastating losses at the Battle of Xiaoting in 222 CE and the subsequent deaths of many founding generals.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Guan Xing was a competent official and military figure who contributed to the stability of Shu Han during the tumultuous Three Kingdoms period. His greater significance, however, lies in his profound cultural impact through his romanticized portrayal in "Romance of the Three Kingdoms," which cemented his image as a loyal warrior for centuries.
